ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Neurology (epilepsy) Consultation — Bruce Lee

code.originalText: Epilepsy clinic: MRI brain with epilepsy protocol, sleep-deprived EEG, classification, and the decision on an antiseizure medicine

text.paragraph: First convulsive collapse four days ago in a 32-year-old martial artist and actor, after a week of short sleep, missed meals, hours in a hot recording booth and cannabis the same morning. Please see him this week to confirm whether this was a seizure, complete the evaluation and advise on an antiseizure medicine, driving and work safety. [S]

list.item: Was this an epileptic seizure or convulsive syncope, and how should it be classified?
Do you agree with MRI with an epilepsy protocol and an EEG, and what do they show?
Is this an unprovoked seizure, given the sleep loss, heat, missed meals and cannabis, and does he have epilepsy?
Should he start an antiseizure medicine now, and if not, what would change that?
What should he be told about driving under Hong Kong rules, stunt work, cannabis, fluids and the medicines he should avoid, including for his back pain?

text.paragraph: Bruce Lee, a 32-year-old martial artist, actor and film-maker, is seen at the request of Dr. Cheung-Hartley eight days after a first convulsive event at a film studio. He remembers feeling hot, light-headed and nauseated in the restroom after a long session in a hot recording booth, and nothing more until he was in the ambulance. A colleague, by telephone at his request, describes him sinking to the floor, stiffening with flexed arms, then rhythmic jerking of all limbs for about a minute with the eyes open, vomiting, and confusion for about 20 minutes; the onset was not seen. Triggers that day: a week of about four hours of sleep a night, little food, a large water intake in the heat, and cannabis that morning. No previous seizure, febrile seizure, head injury with loss of consciousness, central nervous system infection, staring spells or jerks on waking; no family history of epilepsy or of sudden death at a young age. Chronic back pain since a lifting injury three years ago; acetaminophen only. He wants to understand the evidence and decide for himself. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Bruce Jun Fan Lee was born on November 27, 1940, at the Jackson Street Hospital in San Francisco's Chinatown, while his parents were on tour with the Chinese opera; his parents named him Jun Fan, and a nurse at the hospital gave him the English name Bruce. At three months old he returned with his parents to Hong Kong, where he was raised until the age of 18. [D]
His Chinese name was 李振藩 (Lee Jun-fan in Cantonese romanization); as a child actor he took the stage name 李小龍 (Lee Siu-lung, "Little Dragon"). [D]
Raised in Hong Kong, he was a child actor in some 20 films; at 13 he began studying wing chun gung fu under Yip Man, and he was also an accomplished dancer. [D]

In 1959 he returned to the United States, settled in Seattle, studied philosophy at the University of Washington and began teaching gung fu, opening schools in Seattle, Oakland and Los Angeles; he developed his own martial art, Jeet Kune Do ("the way of the intercepting fist"), grounded in simplicity, directness and personal freedom. He is known for the words "Be water, my friend." [D]

In 1970, without warming up, he lifted a 125-pound barbell in a "good morning" exercise and severely injured his back; after many tests an injury to the fourth sacral nerve was found. He was ordered to complete bed rest, told he would never do gung fu again, and stayed in bed for about six months before beginning his own recovery program; the injury became a chronic source of pain for the rest of his life. [D]

He returned to Hong Kong to make films for Golden Harvest: The Big Boss (1971), Fist of Fury and The Way of the Dragon, which he wrote, directed and starred in; Enter the Dragon, the first Hong Kong and Hollywood co-production, was released after his death. [D]

On May 10, 1973, while dubbing lines for Enter the Dragon at Golden Harvest's Hammer Hill Road studios in Hong Kong, he felt faint, collapsed in the bathroom, was helped back to the dubbing studio, vomited and fainted again; he was taken to hospital in critical condition, where a neurosurgeon diagnosed cerebral oedema and gave mannitol to reduce the swelling. He recovered. [D]

His biographer Matthew Polly, as quoted in the Clinical Kidney Journal, wrote that on May 10 "his body began convulsing" after he lost consciousness; a seizure was considered a potential cause of the episode, but because it was a single episode, epilepsy was not diagnosed. [D]

The air conditioning in the dubbing room had been turned off to avoid sound problems in the recording, and he had high temperature, weakness, vomiting and loss of consciousness, according to his biographer. [D]
He had used cannabis (hashish) on the day of the May 10 collapse; the Hong Kong neurosurgeon who treated him thought it was a factor, an explanation he rejected. [D]
His biographer reported that some months before May 1973 he had the sweat glands removed from his armpits. [D]

He married in 1964; a son was born in 1965 and a daughter in 1969. His father, the Cantonese opera performer and actor Lee Hoi Chuen, died in Hong Kong in 1965, a week after the birth of his first grandchild. [D]

text.paragraph: No results recorded at this visit.

list.item: Seizure, not syncope; classification (R56.9). An epileptic seizure. The prodrome of heat and faintness could fit syncope, but a minute of rhythmic jerking, vomiting and 20 minutes of confusion do not: convulsive syncope causes brief, irregular jerks and a quick recovery. The ECG gives no cardiac cause. By the ILAE 2017 classification it is an unknown-onset motor (tonic-clonic) seizure, because its onset was not witnessed and the EEG shows no focal features. [S]

Evaluation (R56.9). Yes, both are indicated after a first seizure. The MRI with an epilepsy protocol shows no hippocampal sclerosis, malformation, tumor or scar, and the sleep-deprived EEG has no epileptiform discharges. [S]

Unprovoked; not epilepsy (R56.9). An acute symptomatic seizure requires a severe metabolic disturbance, intoxication or withdrawal, or an acute brain insult. His sodium, glucose and calcium were normal, and the cannabis did not amount to intoxication by his account; cannabis is not an established epileptogenic drug. Sleep loss, heat and missed meals lower the threshold but do not make the seizure provoked. This is a first unprovoked seizure. With a single seizure, a normal EEG and MRI, and no earlier brain insult, he does not meet the ILAE definition of epilepsy. [S]

Antiseizure medicine (R56.9). Not now, which he chose after hearing the evidence. Adults with a first unprovoked seizure have a 21% to 45% risk of another within two years, and his normal EEG and MRI, daytime seizure and lack of a prior brain insult put him at the lower end. Immediate treatment would lower the two-year risk but not the chance of long-term remission, and side effects affect 7% to 31% of people. A second unprovoked seizure, or an epileptiform EEG on any repeat study, would mean epilepsy and starting a medicine such as levetiracetam or lamotrigine. [S]

Driving, work and medicine safety (R56.9). Hong Kong's licence regulations list epilepsy and liability to sudden fainting among the conditions for which a licence must be refused or cancelled; I advise no driving for at least six months, as many licensing authorities require after a first unprovoked seizure, and then a review. No work at heights, falls or swimming alone until six months; sparring and training are fine once his back allows. No cannabis for now, which he chose. Drink to thirst with salt or an electrolyte drink in the heat, not large volumes of plain water. For his back, avoid tramadol and bupropion, which lower the seizure threshold, and carisoprodol or meprobamate, whose withdrawal can cause seizures; acetaminophen, short courses of an anti-inflammatory and exercise therapy are safe. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Cheung-Hartley's note. Emergency department: sodium 136 mmol/L, glucose 104 mg/dL, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, creatine kinase 2,400 U/L; CT of the head normal; ECG sinus tachycardia with a normal QTc. Clinic four days later: sodium 139, potassium 4.1, calcium 9.5 and magnesium 2.0, creatinine 1.02 mg/dL, creatine kinase 820 U/L, TSH 1.6; ECG sinus bradycardia 56 with QTc 412 ms and no pre-excitation or Brugada pattern. Today: MRI of the brain with an epilepsy protocol, normal; sleep-deprived EEG with wakefulness, drowsiness and light sleep, hyperventilation and photic stimulation, normal. [S]

list.item: No antiseizure medicine after this first unprovoked seizure; start one after a second unprovoked seizure. [S]
No repeat MRI or EEG unless there is a new event. [S]
No driving for at least six months, then review under the Hong Kong rules. [S]
No work at heights, stunt falls or swimming alone for six months; seizure first aid for colleagues. [S]
At least seven hours of sleep, regular meals, breaks and air conditioning during long sessions, and drinking to thirst with electrolytes in the heat. [S]
No cannabis while the risk is highest. [S]
Avoid tramadol, bupropion, carisoprodol and meprobamate; acetaminophen, short anti-inflammatory courses and exercise therapy for the back. [S]
Repeat creatine kinase and creatinine until normal. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Cheung-Hartley the same day. The results and the choice about medicine were explained to Bruce Lee, who asked detailed questions and made the decision himself; he will decide what to share with his family. [S]
Follow-up: Dr. Cheung-Hartley continues his care with reviews at one and two months. Epilepsy clinic review at six months, or at once with any event. [S]
